claim: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is an autoimmune disease caused by loss of pancreatic β cells via apoptosis while neighboring α cells are preserved.
source: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is an autoimmune disease caused by loss of pancreatic β cells via apoptosis while neighboring α cells are preserved.
evidence: This is a well-established characterization of T1D supported by scientific consensus and citations in the manuscript.

claim: Viral infections by coxsackieviruses (CVB) may contribute to trigger autoimmunity in T1D.
source: Viral infections by coxsackieviruses (CVB) may contribute to trigger autoimmunity in T1D.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations throughout the manuscript discussing epidemiological and clinical evidence.

claim: Global gene expression is similar in cytokine-treated and virus-infected human islet cells.
source: We presently describe that global gene expression is similar in cytokine-treated and virus-infected human islet cells, with up-regulation of gene networks involved in cell autonomous immune responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by microarray and RNAseq data presented in Figure 1 and related analyses.

claim: α cells trigger a more efficient antiviral response than β cells.
source: Comparison between the responses of rat pancreatic α and β cells to infection by CVB5 and 4 indicate that α cells trigger a more efficient antiviral response than β cells, including higher basal and induced expression of STAT1-regulated genes, and are thus better able to clear viral infections than β cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing α and β cell responses to CVB infection, including gene expression and viral clearance measurements.

claim: α cells have higher basal and induced expression of STAT1-regulated genes compared to β cells.
source: Comparison between the responses of rat pancreatic α and β cells to infection by CVB5 and 4 indicate that α cells trigger a more efficient antiviral response than β cells, including higher basal and induced expression of STAT1-regulated genes, and are thus better able to clear viral infections than β cells.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR and Western blot data shown in Figures 6, 9, and 10.

claim: The disease is characterized by pancreatic islet inflammation (insulitis) and progressive β cell loss by apoptosis.
source: The disease is characterized by pancreatic islet inflammation (insulitis) and progressive β cell loss by apoptosis (Ziegler and Nepom, 2010; Morgan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on T1D pathology.

claim: The triggering of T1D probably depends on environmental factors that interact with predisposing genes to induce autoimmunity against the β cells.
source: The triggering of T1D probably depends on environmental factors that interact with predisposing genes to induce autoimmunity against the β cells (Eizirik et al., 2009; Santin and Eizirik, 2013; Morgan and Richardson, 2014; Morgan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations discussing the multifactorial etiology of T1D.

claim: CVB-specific antibodies and enteroviral RNA are more frequently observed in serum samples from T1D patients than in healthy individuals.
source: CVB-specific antibodies and enteroviral RNA are more frequently observed in serum samples from T1D patients than in healthy individuals (Helfand et al., 1995; Lonnrot et al., 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: The enteroviral capsid protein VP1 is present at a higher frequency in insulin-containing islets from patients with recent-onset T1D when compared to healthy controls.
source: staining of human pancreatic islets revealed that the enteroviral capsid protein VP1 is present at a higher frequency in insulin-containing islets from patients with recent-onset T1D when compared to healthy controls (Dotta et al., 2007; Richardson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to histological studies.

claim: A meta-analysis of 33 prevalence studies involving 1931 T1D cases and 2517 controls confirmed a clinically significant association between enteroviral infections and islet autoimmunity and T1D in humans.
source: A meta-analysis of 33 prevalence studies involving 1931 T1D cases and 2517 controls confirmed a clinically significant association between enteroviral infections and islet autoimmunity and T1D in humans (Yeung et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a meta-analysis.

claim: The presence of enterovirus RNA in blood can predict the development of T1D.
source: it has been shown that the presence of enterovirus RNA (Oikarinen et al., 2011) or antibodies anti-CVB1 (Laitinen et al., 2014) in blood can predict the development of T1D.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to predictive studies.

claim: Antibodies anti-CVB1 in blood can predict the development of T1D.
source: it has been shown that the presence of enterovirus RNA (Oikarinen et al., 2011) or antibodies anti-CVB1 (Laitinen et al., 2014) in blood can predict the development of T1D.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a predictive study.

claim: Pro-inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1β (IL-1β), type II interferon (IFNγ), and tumor necrosis factor α are released by immune cells closely to the target cells.
source: The immune cells cause selective β cell destruction both directly and via the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin-1β (IL-1β), type II interferon (IFNγ), and tumor necrosis factor α. These cytokines are released closely to the target cells and modulate the expression of complex gene networks in β cells
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge of immune cell function in T1D.

claim: Pro-inflammatory cytokines modulate the expression of complex gene networks in β cells, leading to the release of chemokines and eventually to the activation of the intrinsic pathway of cell death in β cells.
source: These cytokines are released closely to the target cells and modulate the expression of complex gene networks in β cells, leading to the release of chemokines and eventually to the activation of the intrinsic pathway of cell death in β cells (Eizirik et al., 2009; Gurzov and Eizirik, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on cytokine effects on β cells.

claim: Cerebellum granule cell neurons and cortical neurons (CNs) have unique self-defense programs that confer differential resistance to infection by West Nile virus.
source: It has been shown that cerebellum granule cell neurons and cortical neurons (CNs) have unique self-defense programs that confer differential resistance to infection by West Nile virus.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study on neuronal antiviral responses.

claim: Higher basal expression and faster up-regulation of IFN-induced genes improves the survival of granule cell neurons infected by West Nile virus.
source: Specifically, higher basal expression and faster up-regulation of IFN-induced genes improves the survival of granule cell neurons infected by West Nile virus (Cho et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study on neuronal antiviral responses.

claim: Several candidate genes for T1D expressed in human islets, such as the RIG-like receptor MDA5 and the regulators of type I IFNs PTPN2 and USP18, modulate viral detection, antiviral activity, and innate immunity.
source: Several candidate genes for T1D expressed in human islets, such as the RIG-like receptor MDA5 (Colli et al., 2010) and the regulators of type I IFNs PTPN2 and USP18 (Moore et al., 2009; Colli et al., 2010; Santin et al., 2012), modulate viral detection, antiviral activity, and innate immunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on T1D candidate genes.

claim: The candidate genes MDA5, PTPN2, USP18 and CVB5 infection regulate β cell apoptosis via activation of the BH3-only protein Bim.
source: The candidate genes described above (Moore et al., 2009; Colli et al., 2010; Santin et al., 2012) and CVB5 infection (Colli et al., 2011) regulate β cell apoptosis via activation of the BH3-only protein Bim.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on β cell apoptosis mechanisms.

claim: Comparison of human islets exposed to cytokines and analyzed by either microarray or RNAseq showed a strong similarity in the top 20% ranked genes (50% common genes).
source: Comparison of human islets exposed to cytokines and analyzed by either microarray or RNAseq showed a strong similarity in the top 20% ranked genes (50% common genes; Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis presented in Figure 1.

claim: Comparison between CBV5-infected human islets against cytokine-treated human islets indicated a large number of common genes, in particular among the top 20% genes (30–50% common genes).
source: Comparison between CBV5-infected human islets against cytokine-treated human islets indicated a large number of common genes, in particular among the top 20% genes (30–50% common genes).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis presented in Figure 1.

claim: The AUC for a comparison between different batches of human islets exposed to cytokines and analyzed either by microarray or RNAseq analysis was 0.209.
source: Interestingly, the area under the curve (AUC) for a comparison between different batches of human islets exposed to cytokines and analyzed either by microarray or RNAseq analysis was 0.209 (subtracted by a null area of 0.5)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the gene expression ranking similarity analysis.

claim: The AUC for the comparisons virus vs cytokines (microarray vs microarray or microarray vs RNAseq) was, respectively, 0.154 and 0.127.
source: while the AUC for the comparisons virus vs cytokines (microarray vs microarray or microarray vs RNAseq) was, respectively, 0.154 and 0.127
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the gene expression ranking similarity analysis.

claim: There was limited similarity between virus- and palmitate-induced genes, with a curve close to random and an AUC of 0.027.
source: There was limited similarity between virus- and palmitate-induced genes, with a curve close to random (Figure 1) and an AUC of 0.027
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis presented in Figure 1.

claim: Cytokine-exposed human islets highly express and up-regulate antiviral factors.
source: By further comparing the RNAseq data obtained in human islets (Eizirik et al., 2012; Lopes et al., 2014) against known PRRs and other antiviral/antibacterial factors (Randow et al., 2013; Carty et al., 2014), we noticed that cytokine-exposed human islets highly express and up-regulate antiviral (e.g., TLR3, MDA5, RIG-1, APOBEC36, SAMHD1, TRIM22, CNP, Tetherin, Viperin etc) factors
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data analysis comparing against known antiviral factors.

claim: Antibacterial factors are lowly or not expressed in cytokine-exposed human islets.
source: while antibacterial factors (e.g., TLR4, NLRP1, CLEC6A, CLEC7A.) are lowly or not expressed
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data analysis.

claim: Human islet cells are under evolutionary pressure to counteract viral but not bacterial infections.
source: suggesting that these cells are under evolutionary pressure to counteract viral but not bacterial infections, probably because they are seldom confronted by bacteria.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential expression of antiviral vs antibacterial factors.

claim: Pathway analysis of genes induced in common by cytokines and viral infection indicated presence of large groups of genes involved in interferon signaling.
source: Pathway analysis of genes induced in common by cytokines and viral infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3; for clarity only the top 30 correlations are shown) indicated presence of large groups of genes involved in interferon signaling (top correlation for both cytokine data sets compared to the virus data set)
evidence: This claim is supported by IPA pathway analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Both β and α cells were killed to a same extent after a 24 hr exposure to different concentrations of IL-1β + IFNγ.
source: Both β and α cells were killed to a same extent after a 24 hr exposure to different concentrations of IL-1β + IFNγ (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by apoptosis data shown in Figure 3A and supplementary figure.

claim: FACS-purified rat α and β cells are similarly affected by cytokine-induced apoptosis under the present experimental conditions.
source: indicating that under the present experimental conditions FACS-purified rat α and β cells are similarly affected by cytokine-induced apoptosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the apoptosis data in Figure 3A.

claim: β and α cells showed roughly similar iNOS expression and medium nitrite accumulation, with slightly higher nitrite production by β cells.
source: One of the mechanisms involved in cytokine-induced cell death is NO production (Eizirik and Mandrup-Poulsen, 2001), and β and α cells showed roughly similar iNOS expression and medium nitrite accumulation, with slightly higher nitrite production by β cells, but basal iNOS expression was higher in α than β cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by iNOS expression and nitrite measurement data in supplementary figure.

claim: Basal iNOS expression was higher in α than β cells.
source: but basal iNOS expression was higher in α than β cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by iNOS expression data in supplementary figure.

claim: Cytokines induced expression of the chemokines CXCL10 and CCL2 in both β and α cell types.
source: Similarly, cytokines induced expression of the chemokines CXCL10 and CCL2 in both cell types, but CCL2 expression was higher in α cells basally and following cytokine-exposure (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by chemokine expression data in supplementary figure.

claim: CCL2 expression was higher in α cells basally and following cytokine-exposure.
source: but CCL2 expression was higher in α cells basally and following cytokine-exposure (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by chemokine expression data in supplementary figure.

claim: The synthetic dsRNA polyinosinic-polycitidilic acid (PIC) induced a similar percentage of cell death in β and α cells.
source: In line with the cytokine data, the synthetic dsRNA polyinosinic-polycitidilic acid (PIC) induced a similar percentage of cell death in β and α cells (Figure 3B)
evidence: This claim is supported by apoptosis data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PIC induced slightly higher expression of IFNα in α compared to β cells.
source: but a slightly higher expression of the downstream genes IFNα (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B) and CCL2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3F) in α compared to β cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data in supplementary figure.

claim: PIC induced slightly higher expression of CCL2 in α compared to β cells.
source: but a slightly higher expression of the downstream genes IFNα (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B) and CCL2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3F) in α compared to β cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data in supplementary figure.

claim: Basal expression of the transcription factor STAT1 was higher in α than in β cells.
source: Furthermore, basal expression of the transcription factor STAT1, iNOS and of the chemokines CXCL10 and CCL2 was also higher in α than in β cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data in supplementary figure.

claim: Basal expression of CXCL10 was higher in α than in β cells.
source: Furthermore, basal expression of the transcription factor STAT1, iNOS and of the chemokines CXCL10 and CCL2 was also higher in α than in β cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data in supplementary figure.

claim: Infection of β and α cells with CVB5 at a multiplicity of infection (M.O.I.) 5 induced death of nearly 50% of β cells after 36 hr.
source: In contrast with the observations made with cytokines and dsRNA (see above), infection of these cells with CVB5 at a multiplicity of infection (M.O.I.) 5 induced death of nearly 50% of β cells after 36 hr
evidence: This claim is supported by apoptosis data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: CVB5 infection at M.O.I. 5 did not increase α cell death at 36 hr post-infection.
source: but it did not increase α cell death at this time point (Figure 3C) or after a more prolonged follow-up (up to 96 hr) post-infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by apoptosis data shown in Figure 3C and supplementary figure.

claim: UV-inactivated virus did not kill β cells.
source: UV-inactivated virus did not kill β cells (Figure 3—figures supplement 5), indicating that cell death is the consequence of actual viral infection and proliferation.
evidence: This claim is supported by apoptosis data with UV-inactivated virus in supplementary figure.

claim: Cell death from CVB5 is the consequence of actual viral infection and proliferation.
source: UV-inactivated virus did not kill β cells (Figure 3—figures supplement 5), indicating that cell death is the consequence of actual viral infection and proliferation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the UV-inactivation experiment.

claim: There were no differences in the number of α cells attached to the well before and after CVB5 infection.
source: Additionally, there were no differences in the number of α cells attached to the well before and after the infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 6), supporting the assumption that the α cells remain alive after CVB5 infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell counting data in supplementary figure.

claim: α cells resistance to CVB5 was independent of the glucose/fetal bovine serum (FBS) concentration used in the medium.
source: α cells resistance was independent of the glucose/fetal bovine serum (FBS) concentration used in the medium (Figure 3—figure supplement 7)
evidence: This claim is supported by apoptosis data under different culture conditions in supplementary figure.

claim: α cells resistance to CVB5 was paralleled by a markedly lower expression of the CVB5 marker VP1 in α than in β cells, as evaluated by mRNA.
source: and it was paralleled by a markedly lower expression of the CVB5 marker VP1 in α than in β cells, as evaluated by mRNA (Figure 3D) and protein (Figure 3E,F) expression, and by titration of the production of infective virus (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by VP1 mRNA expression data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: α cells resistance to CVB5 was paralleled by a markedly lower expression of the CVB5 marker VP1 in α than in β cells, as evaluated by protein expression.
source: and it was paralleled by a markedly lower expression of the CVB5 marker VP1 in α than in β cells, as evaluated by mRNA (Figure 3D) and protein (Figure 3E,F) expression, and by titration of the production of infective virus (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by VP1 protein expression data shown in Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: α cells resistance to CVB5 was paralleled by lower production of infective virus compared to β cells.
source: and it was paralleled by a markedly lower expression of the CVB5 marker VP1 in α than in β cells, as evaluated by mRNA (Figure 3D) and protein (Figure 3E,F) expression, and by titration of the production of infective virus (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral titration data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Even at a M.O.I. of 100, CVB5 still induced markedly less cell death in α than in β cells infected at an M.O.I. 20-fold lower (M.O.I. 5).
source: Dose-response experiments in α cells indicated that even at a M.O.I. of 100, CVB5 still induced markedly less cell death in α than in β cells infected at an M.O.I. 20-fold lower, that is, M.O.I. 5 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response apoptosis data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: α cells were much more resistant than β cells to CVB4-induced cell death.
source: This is not a phenomenon restricted to CVB5, since α cells were also much more resistant than β cells to CVB4-induced cell death (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by apoptosis data with CVB4 shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The CVB receptors coxsackievirus and adenovirus receptor (CAR) and decay accelerating factor for complement have similar or higher mRNA expression in rat α as compared to β cells.
source: This cannot be explained by different expression of receptors for the virus, since the CVB receptors coxsackievirus and adenovirus receptor (CAR) and decay accelerating factor for complement have similar or higher mRNA expression in rat α as compared to β cells (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by receptor mRNA expression data shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: The similar expression of CAR was confirmed at the protein level in α and β cells.
source: The similar expression of CAR was confirmed at the protein level in α and β cells (Figure 4—figures supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in supplementary figure.

claim: The same quantity of CVB5 remained associated with α and β cells after adsorption of the virus as measured by titration 2 hr after virus exposure.
source: Consistently, the same quantity of CVB5 remained associated with α and β cells after adsorption of the virus as measured by titration 2 hr after virus exposure (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is stated but data is not shown in the manuscript.

claim: The percentage of infected α and β cells by a non-replicating adenoviral vector encoding GFP was similar in α and β cells.
source: In line with these findings, the percentage of infected α and β cells by a non-replicating adenoviral vector encoding GFP, which also enters the cells via CAR, was similar in α and β cells (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 5A-C.

claim: The intensity of GFP fluorescence was several-fold lower in α than in β cells after adenoviral infection.
source: On the other hand, the intensity of GFP fluorescence was several-fold lower in α than in β cells (Figure 5A,B,D), indicating that the virus enters α cells but cannot properly translate its cargo protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence intensity data shown in Figures 5A, B, and D.

claim: The virus enters α cells but cannot properly translate its cargo protein.
source: indicating that the virus enters α cells but cannot properly translate its cargo protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of similar infection rates but lower GFP expression in α cells.

claim: α cells have higher basal expression of the chemokines CXCL10 and CCL2 compared to β cells.
source: In comparison to β cells, α cells have higher basal expression of the chemokines CXCL10 and CCL2, of the cytokines IFNα and IL-1β (Figure 6B)
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: α cells have higher basal expression of the cytokines IFNα and IL-1β compared to β cells.
source: In comparison to β cells, α cells have higher basal expression of the chemokines CXCL10 and CCL2, of the cytokines IFNα and IL-1β (Figure 6B)
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: α cells have higher basal expression of the transcription factor STAT1 compared to β cells.
source: of the transcription factor STAT1 (which mediates IFN signal transduction) and of several IFN-related downstream genes previously described to have a role in cell autonomous immune response in the brain (Cho et al., 2013), including Viperin, Tetherin, PKR, Mx1, USP18, Oas1, and so on (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: α cells have higher basal expression of several IFN-related downstream genes including Viperin, Tetherin, PKR, Mx1, USP18, Oas1 compared to β cells.
source: of the transcription factor STAT1 (which mediates IFN signal transduction) and of several IFN-related downstream genes previously described to have a role in cell autonomous immune response in the brain (Cho et al., 2013), including Viperin, Tetherin, PKR, Mx1, USP18, Oas1, and so on (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Several IFN-related genes have higher expression in granule cell neurons of the cerebellum compared to cortical neurons, explaining why these cells are more resistant to infection by positive-stranded RNA viruses.
source: Several of these genes have higher expression in granule cell neurons of the cerebellum, as compared to CNs, explaining why these cells are more resistant to infection by positive-stranded RNA viruses (Cho et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study on neuronal antiviral responses.

claim: There is remarkable similarity between gene expression in neurons and β cells.
source: There is remarkable similarity between gene expression in neurons and β cells (Atouf et al., 1997; Villate et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies comparing neuronal and β cell gene expression.

claim: 64% of cell autonomous immune response genes were similarly increased in both granule neurons and α cells.
source: The data shown in Figure 7 and Supplementary file 1 indicate a clear similarity between granule neurons and α cells for the genes present in both data sets; indeed, 64% of these genes were similarly increased in both cell types, with only 4% showing opposite direction of expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 7 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Only 4% of cell autonomous immune response genes showed opposite direction of expression between granule neurons and α cells.
source: indeed, 64% of these genes were similarly increased in both cell types, with only 4% showing opposite direction of expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 7 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Following a 36 hr infection with CVB5, α cells presented higher levels of the viral sensors MDA5 and PKR compared to β cells.
source: Following a 36 hr infection of α and β cells with CVB5 (Figure 8), α cells presented higher levels of the viral sensors MDA5 and PKR, of iNOS and CCL2, but lower induction of Viperin.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Following a 36 hr infection with CVB5, α cells presented higher levels of iNOS and CCL2 compared to β cells.
source: Following a 36 hr infection of α and β cells with CVB5 (Figure 8), α cells presented higher levels of the viral sensors MDA5 and PKR, of iNOS and CCL2, but lower induction of Viperin.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Following a 36 hr infection with CVB5, α cells presented lower induction of Viperin compared to β cells.
source: Following a 36 hr infection of α and β cells with CVB5 (Figure 8), α cells presented higher levels of the viral sensors MDA5 and PKR, of iNOS and CCL2, but lower induction of Viperin.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 8.

claim: A time-course analysis showed a progressive increase in the viral capsid protein VP1 in β cells infected with CVB5.
source: A time-course analysis of α and β cells infected with CVB5 showed a progressive increase in the viral capsid protein VP1 in β cells (Figure 9A)
evidence: This claim is supported by time-course VP1 expression data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: There was an early increase in VP1 expression in α cells infected with CVB5, with peak at 8 hr and subsequent decrease by 24 hr.
source: while there was an early increase in VP1 expression in α cells (see inset in Figure 9A), with peak at 8 hr and subsequent decrease by 24 hr, suggesting that these cells are indeed infected by CVB5 but manage to eradicate the virus without dying.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-course VP1 expression data shown in Figure 9A inset.

claim: α cells are indeed infected by CVB5 but manage to eradicate the virus without dying.
source: suggesting that these cells are indeed infected by CVB5 but manage to eradicate the virus without dying.
evidence: This is an inference based on the transient VP1 expression pattern in α cells.

claim: α cells have both a higher basal expression and induction of STAT1 mRNA compared to β cells.
source: In line with this, α cells have both a higher basal expression and induction of two mRNAs encoding key antiviral proteins, namely STAT1 (Figure 9B) and MX1 (Figure 9C) as compared to β cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-course STAT1 expression data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: α cells have both a higher basal expression and induction of MX1 mRNA compared to β cells.
source: In line with this, α cells have both a higher basal expression and induction of two mRNAs encoding key antiviral proteins, namely STAT1 (Figure 9B) and MX1 (Figure 9C) as compared to β cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-course MX1 expression data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Knockdown of STAT1 in α cells prevented MX1 up-regulation in response to CVB5 infection.
source: Knockdown of STAT1 in α cells by a previously validated (Moore et al., 2011) siRNA (Figure 10D) prevented MX1 up-regulation in response to CVB5 infection (Figure 10E)
evidence: This claim is supported by siRNA knockdown experiment data shown in Figures 10D and 10E.

claim: Knockdown of STAT1 in α cells enabled a more intense CVB5 infection, as indicated by increased VP1 expression.
source: and enabled a more intense CVB5 infection, as indicated by increased VP1 expression (Figure 10F).
evidence: This claim is supported by siRNA knockdown experiment data shown in Figure 10F.

claim: STAT1 plays a key role in α cell resistance to viral infection.
source: These observations confirm that STAT1 plays a key role in α cell resistance to viral infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the STAT1 knockdown experiments.

claim: Human β cells are more sensitive than α cells to CVB-induced infection and functional impairment both in vivo and in vitro.
source: It has been previously shown that human β cells are more sensitive than α cells to CVB-induced infection and functional impairment both in vivo and in vitro (Dotta et al., 2007; Richardson et al., 2009; Anagandula et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CVB does not infect human α cells during the progression of T1D.
source: leading to the suggestion that CVB does not infect human α cells during the progression of T1D.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous literature that the authors are challenging.

claim: α cells may become infected but are able to eradicate the virus more effectively than β cells.
source: Our present findings suggest an alternative hypothesis, namely that α cells may become infected but are able to eradicate the virus more effectively than β cells (see Figure 9).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their experimental findings.

claim: 52% (human islet sample 1) and 33% (human islet sample 2) insulin-positive cells were also positive for VP1 after CVB5 infection for 8 hr.
source: Thus, 52% (human islet sample 1) and 33% (human islet sample 2) insulin-positive cells were also positive for VP1, while 28% (human islet sample 1) or 27% (human islet sample 2) of cells were double positive for glucagon and VP1 (Figure 11).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 11.

claim: 28% (human islet sample 1) or 27% (human islet sample 2) of cells were double positive for glucagon and VP1 after CVB5 infection for 8 hr.
source: Thus, 52% (human islet sample 1) and 33% (human islet sample 2) insulin-positive cells were also positive for VP1, while 28% (human islet sample 1) or 27% (human islet sample 2) of cells were double positive for glucagon and VP1 (Figure 11).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 11.

claim: The enteroviral capsid protein VP1 was detected in β cells in all three cases of children who died from myocarditis during acute CVB infection.
source: To confirm these results in clinically relevant samples, we examined the pancreas of three children who died from myocarditis during the course of an acute and severe CVB infection. In these samples, we detected the presence of the enteroviral capsid protein, VP1, in β cells in all three cases and in α cells in two of three cases (Figure 12 and Figure 12—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from human pancreas samples shown in Figure 12.

claim: The enteroviral capsid protein VP1 was detected in α cells in two of three cases of children who died from myocarditis during acute CVB infection.
source: In these samples, we detected the presence of the enteroviral capsid protein, VP1, in β cells in all three cases and in α cells in two of three cases (Figure 12 and Figure 12—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from human pancreas samples shown in Figure 12.

claim: In patients with acute CVB infection, the number of infected α cells was clearly lower than the number of infected β cells.
source: In these latter patients, the number of infected α cells was clearly lower than the number of infected β cells.
evidence: This is an observation from the immunofluorescence analysis of human pancreas samples.

claim: The immune-related gene networks in β cells are part of a complex cell autonomous immune response aiming to eradicate putative viral infections without excessive cell loss.
source: The present observations, indicating a close similarity between cytokine- and virus-induced gene expression, suggest that these gene networks are actually part of a complex cell autonomous immune response, regulated at least in part by candidate genes for T1D (Santin and Eizirik, 2013), aiming to eradicate putative viral infections without excessive cell loss.
evidence: This is an interpretation and hypothesis based on the gene expression similarity data.

claim: β cells have a very limited replication potential.
source: Indeed, β cells, like neurons, have a very limited replication potential (Cnop et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established knowledge about β cell biology.

claim: An excessive loss of β cells would be disastrous for the host.
source: and an excessive loss of β cells would be disastrous for the host.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the essential role of β cells in glucose homeostasis.

claim: In some genetically susceptible individuals, the putative initial viral infection might not be resolved leading to a persistent low-level infection, which could trigger a specific autoimmune assault against β cells.
source: In some genetically susceptible individuals, however, the putative initial viral infection might not be resolved leading to a persistent low-level infection, which in these individuals could trigger a specific autoimmune assault against β cells (Dotta et al., 2007; Santin and Eizirik, 2013; Richardson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings and supported by citations.

claim: Pancreatic α and β cells are neighboring endocrine cells with a common embryonic origin.
source: Pancreatic α and β cells are neighboring endocrine cells with a common embryonic origin (Teitelman, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to developmental biology literature.

claim: The main difference between α and β cells is not their actual ability to detect signals of the viral infection but how they respond to the virus once it is actively translating proteins inside the cells.
source: This suggests that the main difference between these two cell types is not their actual ability to detect signals of the viral infection (e.g., dsRNA) but how they respond to the virus once it is actively translating proteins inside the cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similar responses to dsRNA but different responses to actual viral infection.

claim: A large number of IFN- and STAT1-dependent genes are expressed at higher level in α cells as compared to β cells.
source: Analysis of the expression of cell autonomous immunity-related genes in α and β cells (present data) and comparison between global expression of these genes in virus-resistant mouse granule cell neurons (Cho et al., 2013) and α cells indicate that a large number of IFN- and STAT1-dependent genes are expressed at higher level in α cells as compared to β cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data presented in Figures 6-8 and comparative analysis with neuronal data.

claim: The IFN-STAT1 gene network contributes to the resistance of α cells to viral infection.
source: This suggests that this IFN-STAT1 gene network contributes to the resistance of α cells to viral infection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the higher expression of IFN-STAT1 genes in α cells and their resistance to viral infection.

claim: Unphosphorylated STAT1 supports the induction of antiviral genes in other cell types even without IFN-dependent stimulation.
source: Of note, unphosphorylated STAT1 supports the induction of antiviral genes in other cell types even without IFN-dependent stimulation (Yang and Stark, 2008; Cheon and Stark, 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on STAT1 function.

claim: Increased basal expression of STAT1 amplifies cell-intrinsic immune responses.
source: and increased basal expression of STAT1 amplifies cell-intrinsic immune responses (Hu et al., 2008; Amit et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on STAT1 function.

claim: Polymorphic variants of MDA5 that reduce helicase activity are associated with a lower risk to develop T1D.
source: Our proposal that a strong cell immune response protects α cells against viral infection and subsequent death in T1D seems at odds with the association of polymorphic variants of MDA5 that reduce helicase activity with a lower risk to develop T1D (Nejentsev et al., 2009; Winkler et al., 2011; Lincez et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to genetic association studies.

claim: The long-lasting detection of enteroviral protein expression and IFN-induced markers in β cells in pre-diabetic or diabetic donors most probably reflects a chronic non-cytolytic infection.
source: The long-lasting detection of enteroviral protein expression and IFN-induced markers in β cells in pre-diabetic or diabetic donors (Dotta et al., 2007; Richardson et al., 2013, 2014); however, most probably reflects a chronic non-cytolytic infection.
evidence: This is an interpretation of published findings supported by citations.

claim: In chronic non-cytolytic infection, the continuous stimulation of vigorous antiviral responses may lead to protracted presentation of β cell autoantigens, local release of chemokines and cytokines and eventually autoimmunity.
source: In this context, the continuous stimulation of vigorous antiviral responses, in an attempt to control the infection, may lead to protracted presentation of β cell autoantigens, local release of chemokines and cytokines and eventually autoimmunity (Santin and Eizirik, 2013).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis proposed by the authors and supported by citation.

claim: The process of chronic infection leading to autoimmunity would not take place in α cells, which have adequate mechanisms to swiftly eliminate the virus in the early stages of infection.
source: This process, however, would not take place in α cells, which, as presently shown, have in place adequate mechanisms to swiftly eliminate the virus in the early stages of infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing α cells can clear viral infection.

claim: Pancreatic α and β cells provide a unique model to understand how molecular regulation of self-defense against viral infection may determine cell death, local inflammation, and eventual diabetes.
source: They thus provide a unique model to understand how molecular regulation of self-defense against viral infection in β cells, as compared to α cells, may determine cell death, local inflammation, and eventual diabetes.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the significance of the model system.

claim: Pancreatic α and β cells have different cell autonomous signatures.
source: The present observations suggest that pancreatic α and β cells have different cell autonomous signatures.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gene expression and functional data presented.

claim: Different cell autonomous signatures may explain the different ability of α and β cells to clear viral infections.
source: This may explain their different ability to clear viral infections and potentially explain why putative chronically infected pancreatic β cells, but not α cells, are targeted by an autoimmune response and killed during T1D.
evidence: This is a concluding hypothesis linking the findings to T1D pathogenesis.

claim: Different cell autonomous signatures may explain why putative chronically infected pancreatic β cells, but not α cells, are targeted by an autoimmune response and killed during T1D.
source: This may explain their different ability to clear viral infections and potentially explain why putative chronically infected pancreatic β cells, but not α cells, are targeted by an autoimmune response and killed during T1D.
evidence: This is a concluding hypothesis linking the findings to T1D pathogenesis.

claim: The AUC for virus vs cytokines comparison was 74% and 61% of the cytokines vs cytokines comparison, indicating a close similarity between human islet cell responses to virus or cytokines.
source: that is, 74% and 61% of the cytokines vs cytokines comparison, indicating a close similarity between human islet cell responses to virus or cytokines.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of AUC values from the gene expression ranking similarity analysis.

source: and an AUC of 0.027, that is, <20% of the area observed when comparing virus- against cytokine-induced genes.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison showing lack of similarity between virus and palmitate responses.

claim: More than 40% of the genes up-regulated in common between virus-infected and cytokine-treated human islets.
source: The superposition of up-regulated genes between virus-infected and cytokine-treated human islets confirmed the similarity between virus- and cytokine-induced genes, with >40% of the genes up-regulated in common between both islet treatments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in supplementary figure.
